putnam-2002-a1.title: A recurrence for $P_n$
putnam-2002-a1.body:
Differentiate $\dfrac{P_n(x)}{(x^k-1)^{n+1}}$:
$$\frac{d}{dx}\frac{P_n(x)}{(x^k-1)^{n+1}} = \frac{(x^k-1)P_n'(x) - (n+1)kx^{k-1}P_n(x)}{(x^k-1)^{n+2}},$$
so we may take $P_{n+1}(x) = (x^k-1)P_n'(x) - (n+1)kx^{k-1}P_n(x)$. (The polynomial $P_n$ is uniquely determined by the $n$-th derivative, so this is the $P_{n+1}$ of the problem.) Setting $x = 1$:
$$P_{n+1}(1) = -(n+1)k\,P_n(1).$$
With $P_0 = 1$, induction gives $P_n(1) = (-k)^n\,n!$.

**Answer:** $P_n(1) = (-k)^n\,n!$.

putnam-2002-a1.title: Leibniz rule near $x=1$
putnam-2002-a1.body:
Write $x^k - 1 = (x-1)q(x)$ with $q(x) = 1+x+\cdots+x^{k-1}$, $q(1) = k$, and let $h = 1/q$, which is smooth near $x=1$ with $h(1) = 1/k$. By the Leibniz rule,
$$\frac{d^n}{dx^n}\left[h(x)(x-1)^{-1}\right] = \sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj h^{(n-j)}(x)\,(-1)^j j!\,(x-1)^{-1-j}.$$
Multiplying by $(x^k-1)^{n+1} = (x-1)^{n+1}q(x)^{n+1}$,
$$P_n(x) = q(x)^{n+1}\sum_{j=0}^n\binom nj h^{(n-j)}(x)(-1)^jj!\,(x-1)^{n-j}$$
near $x=1$ (both sides are continuous at $1$). At $x = 1$ only $j = n$ survives:
$$P_n(1) = k^{n+1}\cdot\frac1k\cdot(-1)^n n! = (-k)^n n! .$$
**Answer:** $P_n(1) = (-k)^n\,n!$.

putnam-2002-a2.title: Great circle and pigeonhole
putnam-2002-a2.body:
Pick two of the five points, $P$ and $Q$. There is a great circle $\Gamma$ through $P$ and $Q$ (the intersection of the sphere with a plane through the centre, $P$ and $Q$; if $P,Q$ are antipodal or equal, any such plane through them works).

$\Gamma$ is the common boundary of two closed hemispheres $H_1, H_2$, whose union is the whole sphere, and both contain $\Gamma$, hence $P$ and $Q$. Each of the remaining three points lies in $H_1$ or in $H_2$, so by the pigeonhole principle two of them lie in the same hemisphere, say $H_1$. Then $H_1$ contains $P$, $Q$ and these two points: four of the five points lie on a closed hemisphere. ∎

putnam-2002-a3.title: Add or remove the average
putnam-2002-a3.body:
Let $\mathcal F$ be the family of nonempty subsets of $\{1,\dots,n\}$ with integer average. If $S\in\mathcal F$ has average $m$, then $\min S\le m\le\max S$, so $m\in\{1,\dots,n\}$.

The singletons $\{1\},\dots,\{n\}$ are in $\mathcal F$. Split the remaining sets of $\mathcal F$ into
- $\mathcal A$: sets not containing their average;
- $\mathcal B$: sets with at least two elements containing their average.

(Every set in $\mathcal F$ that is not a singleton is in exactly one of these, and singletons contain their average, so sets in $\mathcal A$ automatically have at least two elements.)

If $S\in\mathcal A$ has $k$ elements and average $m$, then $S\cup\{m\}$ has sum $km+m$ and $k+1$ elements, so its average is still $m$ and it lies in $\mathcal B$. Conversely, if $T\in\mathcal B$ has $k\ge2$ elements and average $m\in T$, then $T\setminus\{m\}$ is nonempty with sum $km-m$ over $k-1$ elements, average $m$, not containing $m$: it lies in $\mathcal A$. These two maps are inverse to each other, so $|\mathcal A| = |\mathcal B|$.

Therefore $T_n = n + |\mathcal A| + |\mathcal B| = n + 2|\mathcal A|$, and $T_n - n$ is even. ∎

putnam-2002-a4.title: Force a zero row, zero column or zero $2\times2$ block
putnam-2002-a4.body:
**Player 0 wins.** It is enough for Player 0 to fill, with zeros, a whole row, a whole column, or a $2\times2$ submatrix (two rows $\times$ two columns): in the last case those two rows have nonzero entries only in the remaining column, so they are linearly dependent. In each case the determinant is $0$ however the rest is filled.

Let $A_{ij}$ be the entry in row $i$, column $j$. Permuting rows or columns, or transposing, changes the determinant at most by a sign, so we may use these symmetries freely.

1. WLOG Player 1 starts at $A_{11}$. Player 0 plays $A_{22}$.
2. Player 1's second move occupies at most one of $A_{23}$, $A_{32}$. Transposing if necessary (this fixes $A_{11}$ and $A_{22}$), $A_{23}$ is vacant; Player 0 plays $A_{23}$.
3. After Player 1's third move: if $A_{21}$ is vacant, Player 0 plays there and row $2$ is all zeros — win. Otherwise Player 1's three $1$'s are at $A_{11}$, $A_{21}$ and one more cell $w$.
4. The cells $A_{12},A_{13},A_{32},A_{33}$ form a $2\times2$ block (rows $1,3$, columns $2,3$) of which $w$ occupies at most one. Choose a row $i\in\{1,3\}$ and a column $j\in\{2,3\}$ both avoiding $w$. Then $A_{i2}, A_{i3}$ are empty, and the column-$j$ cells $A_{1j}$, $A_{3j}$ are empty. Player 0 plays $A_{ij}$. Now Player 0 has two threats:
   - the other cell of row $i$ in columns $2,3$ would complete the zero $2\times2$ block in rows $\{2,i\}$, columns $\{2,3\}$;
   - the remaining cell of column $j$ (in the row other than $2$ and $i$) would complete a zero column $j$.
5. Player 1 can block only one of these two different cells; Player 0 takes the other with the fourth zero and wins.

**Answer: Player 0** wins, e.g. by the strategy above (answer $A_{11}$ with $A_{22}$, then make zero threats in row 2 and finally a double threat of a zero column and a zero $2\times2$ block).

putnam-2002-a5.title: Induction on $r+s$ (Euclid backwards)
putnam-2002-a5.body:
All $a_n$ are positive integers (by induction on $n$), so the fractions make sense.

**Claim.** For all coprime positive integers $r,s$ there is $n\ge0$ with $a_n = r$ and $a_{n+1} = s$.

Then every positive rational $r/s$ (in lowest terms) equals $a_n/a_{n+1} = a_{N-1}/a_N$ with $N = n+1\ge1$, which proves the statement.

*Proof of the claim,* by induction on $r+s$.
- $r+s = 2$: $r = s = 1$, and $a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = a_{2\cdot0+1} = a_0 = 1$, so $n=0$ works.
- $r+s>2$: coprimality excludes $r = s$.
  - If $r>s$: $(r-s,s)$ is coprime with smaller sum, so some $n$ has $a_n = r-s$, $a_{n+1} = s$. Then $a_{2n+2} = a_n + a_{n+1} = r$ and $a_{2n+3} = a_{2(n+1)+1} = a_{n+1} = s$.
  - If $r<s$: some $n$ has $a_n = r$, $a_{n+1} = s-r$. Then $a_{2n+1} = a_n = r$ and $a_{2n+2} = a_n+a_{n+1} = s$.

This completes the induction. ∎

putnam-2002-a6.title: Group by number of digits
putnam-2002-a6.body:
For $d\ge1$, the integers with exactly $d$ base-$b$ digits are $b^{d-1}\le n\le b^d-1$. Let $H_d = \sum_{n=b^{d-1}}^{b^d-1}\frac1n$. All terms are positive, so regrouping is allowed.

**$b\ge3$: divergence.** Here $1$ and $2$ are one-digit numbers and $f(1) = 1\cdot f(1)$, $f(2) = 2f(1)$, so $f(n) = nf(d(n))$ holds for all $n\ge1$. Comparing with an integral (as $1/x$ is decreasing),
$$H_d > \int_{b^{d-1}}^{b^d}\frac{dx}{x} = \ln b > 1 .$$
If the series converged to $\Sigma$ (necessarily $\Sigma>0$), then
$$\Sigma = \sum_{d\ge1}\frac{1}{f(d)}H_d \ge (\ln b)\sum_{d\ge1}\frac1{f(d)} = (\ln b)\,\Sigma > \Sigma,$$
a contradiction. So the series diverges.

**$b = 2$: convergence.** Now $f(1) = 1$, $f(2) = 2$, $f(3) = 3f(2) = 6$, and for $n\ge4$ (at least $3$ binary digits) $f(n) = nf(d)$ with $d\ge3$. For $i\ge3$ let $S_i = \sum_{n=1}^{2^i-1}\frac1{f(n)}$. Then
$$S_i = 1+\frac12+\frac16 + \sum_{d=3}^{i}\frac1{f(d)}H_d .$$
For $d\ge3$, with $a = 2^{d-1}\ge4$,
$$H_d = \frac1a - \frac1{2a} + \sum_{n=a+1}^{2a}\frac1n < \frac1{2a} + \int_a^{2a}\frac{dx}x \le \frac18 + \ln 2 =: c < 0.82 .$$
The numbers $3,\dots,i$ are among $3,\dots,2^i-1$, so $\sum_{d=3}^i\frac1{f(d)}\le S_i - 1 - \frac12$. Hence
$$S_i < \frac53 + c\left(S_i - \frac32\right)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad S_i < \frac{\frac53 - \frac32c}{1-c} .$$
The partial sums are increasing and bounded, so the series converges (to a value below about $2.42$).

**Answer:** the series converges only for $b = 2$.

putnam-2002-b1.title: Induction: the number of hits is uniform
putnam-2002-b1.body:
**Claim.** For $n\ge2$, after $n$ shots the number of hits is uniformly distributed on $\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$, each value with probability $\frac1{n-1}$.

For $n=2$ she has exactly $1$ hit. Suppose the claim holds for $n$. She has $i$ hits after $n+1$ shots ($1\le i\le n$) either if she had $i-1$ hits and then hit (probability $\frac{i-1}n$), or $i$ hits and then missed (probability $1-\frac in$). So
$$P(i\text{ hits after } n+1) = \frac1{n-1}\left(\frac{i-1}n + \frac{n-i}{n}\right) = \frac1{n-1}\cdot\frac{n-1}{n} = \frac1n$$
(terms with $i-1 = 0$ or $i = n$ have probability factor $0$, consistent with the formula). This proves the claim.

With $n=100$, the probability of exactly $50$ hits is $\frac1{99}$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac1{99}$.

putnam-2002-b1.title: Every sequence with the same counts is equally likely
putnam-2002-b1.body:
Consider shots $3$ to $100$ ($98$ shots), and a particular sequence of them with $h$ hits and $m = 98-h$ misses. Before shot $3+t$ she has taken $t+2$ shots. Whenever she hits for the $u$-th time among these, she had $u$ hits so far (counting the first shot); whenever she misses for the $v$-th time, she had $v$ misses so far. So the probability of the sequence is
$$\frac{(1\cdot2\cdots h)(1\cdot2\cdots m)}{2\cdot3\cdots 99} = \frac{h!\,m!}{99!},$$
independent of the order. There are $\binom{98}{h}$ such sequences, so
$$P(h\text{ hits in shots }3\text{–}100) = \binom{98}{h}\frac{h!\,(98-h)!}{99!} = \frac{98!}{99!} = \frac1{99}.$$
Exactly $50$ hits in $100$ shots means $h = 49$, with probability $\frac1{99}$.

**Answer:** $\dfrac1{99}$.

putnam-2002-b2.title: Start on a face with at least four sides
putnam-2002-b2.body:
We assume, as is implicit, that the polyhedron is connected and that two faces share at most one edge (true for convex polyhedra). Since each vertex has degree $3$, exactly three faces meet at each vertex.

**Lemma.** Some face has at least four edges.
*Proof.* Suppose all faces are triangles. Take a face $F_1 = v_1v_2v_3$. The third edge at $v_1$ goes to a vertex $v_4$, and the three faces at $v_1$ are $v_1v_2v_3$, $v_1v_2v_4$, $v_1v_3v_4$. Then $v_2$ has the three edges $v_2v_1, v_2v_3, v_2v_4$, so its third face is $v_2v_3v_4$. These four triangles already give every one of $v_1,\dots,v_4$ its three edges and every one of the six edges its two faces, so they form a closed surface (a tetrahedron), and by connectedness this is the whole polyhedron. It has only $4$ faces, contradicting the hypothesis. (For convex polyhedra this also follows from Euler's formula: $3V = 2E = 3F$ and $V-E+F = 2$ give $F = 4$.)

**Strategy.** Let $A$ be a face with $k\ge4$ edges, and let $B_1,\dots,B_k$ be the faces across its edges, in cyclic order; they are distinct because two faces share at most one edge. At the vertex of $A$ between the edges shared with $B_i$ and $B_{i+1}$, the three faces are exactly $A$, $B_i$, $B_{i+1}$ (indices mod $k$).

1. The first player signs $A$.
2. The second player signs one face, which is at most one of the $B$'s, say (at worst) $B_j$. Since $k\ge4$, the faces $B_{j+1}, B_{j+2}, B_{j+3}$ are three distinct unsigned faces (if the second player signed no $B$, any three consecutive ones work). The first player signs the middle one, $B_{j+2}$.
3. Now $\{A, B_{j+1}, B_{j+2}\}$ and $\{A, B_{j+2}, B_{j+3}\}$ each share a vertex, and the first player needs only $B_{j+1}$ or $B_{j+3}$. The second player (who has only two signatures, so cannot have won yet) can block only one of them; the first player signs the other on the third move and wins.

So the first player always wins. ∎

putnam-2002-b3.title: Compare power series term by term
putnam-2002-b3.body:
Multiplying by $e$, the inequalities are
$$\frac1{2n} < 1 - e\Big(1-\frac1n\Big)^n < \frac1n\iff 1 - \frac1n < e\Big(1-\frac1n\Big)^n < 1 - \frac1{2n}.$$
All three quantities are positive, so taking logarithms gives the equivalent statement
$$\ln\Big(1-\frac1n\Big) < 1 + n\ln\Big(1-\frac1n\Big) < \ln\Big(1-\frac1{2n}\Big).$$
For $0<x<1$, $-\ln(1-x) = \sum_{i\ge1}\frac{x^i}{i}$ (convergent). Hence
$$1 + n\ln\Big(1-\frac1n\Big) = 1 - \sum_{i\ge1}\frac{1}{i\,n^{i-1}} = -\sum_{i\ge 2}\frac{1}{i\,n^{i-1}} = -\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{1}{(i+1)n^i}.$$
Changing signs, we must show
$$\sum_{i\ge1}\frac{1}{i\,2^in^i} < \sum_{i\ge1}\frac{1}{(i+1)n^i} < \sum_{i\ge1}\frac1{i\,n^i}.$$
Compare coefficients of $n^{-i}$: $\frac{1}{i2^i}\le\frac1{i+1}$ because $i2^i\ge i+1$ (equality only for $i = 1$, strict for $i\ge2$), and $\frac1{i+1}<\frac1i$ for all $i$. All series converge absolutely (as $n\ge2$) and at least one comparison is strict, so both inequalities are strict. ∎

putnam-2002-b4.title: Guess the numbers $\equiv 0,1 \pmod 3$ in order
putnam-2002-b4.body:
**Strategy.** Guess in turn $g_1 = 1,\ g_2 = 3,\ g_3 = 4,\ g_4 = 6,\ \dots$, i.e. $g_{2j-1} = 3j-2$ and $g_{2j} = 3j$, as long as the answer is "higher". As soon as the answer is "lower", the feasible set is a single number; guess it.

Each guess is legal: while all answers are "higher", the feasible set is $\{g_t+1,\dots,2002\}$ and $g_{t+1}>g_t$; the sequence ends with $g_{1335} = 2002$ (since $2002 = 3\cdot 668-2$), so it never leaves $[1,2002]$.

**Outcomes.**
- $n\equiv1\pmod3$, $n = 3j-2$: all earlier guesses are smaller, and $n = g_{2j-1}$ is guessed on turn $2j-1$ (odd). **Win.**
- $n\equiv0\pmod 3$, $n = 3j$: guessed on turn $2j$ (even). Lose.
- $n\equiv2\pmod3$, $n = 3j-1$: $g_{2j-1} = 3j-2$ gets "higher", $g_{2j} = 3j$ gets "lower", so the only feasible number is $3j-1 = n$, guessed on turn $2j+1$ (odd). **Win.**

**Probability.** Among $1,\dots,2002$ there are $667$ multiples of $3$, so we win for $2002-667 = 1335$ values, with probability
$$\frac{1335}{2002} > \frac23\quad\text{since}\quad 3\cdot1335 = 4005 > 4004 = 2\cdot2002. \ ∎$$

putnam-2002-b5.title: Square of a factorial
putnam-2002-b5.body:
Let $N = 2002!$ and, for $d = 1,2,\dots,2002$, let $b_d = \frac Nd - 1$, an integer since $d\mid N$. The $b_d$ are distinct (strictly decreasing in $d$) and $b_d\ge\frac{2002!}{2002} - 1 = 2001! - 1$.

Since $N = d(b_d+1)$,
$$N^2 = d^2(b_d+1)^2 = d^2\,b_d^2 + 2d^2\,b_d + d^2 .$$
The numbers $d^2$ and $2d^2$ satisfy $1\le d^2 < 2d^2 \le 2\cdot2002^2 < 2001!-1\le b_d$, so they are legitimate base-$b_d$ digits and the leading digit is nonzero. Hence $N^2$ written in base $b_d$ is the three-digit string $(d^2,\ 2d^2,\ d^2)$, a palindrome.

Thus $N^2 = (2002!)^2$ is a $3$-digit palindrome in at least $2002$ different bases. ∎

putnam-2002-b6.title: Every linear form divides the determinant
putnam-2002-b6.body:
Work in $\mathbb F_p[x,y,z]$ (reduce coefficients mod $p$); this is a unique factorisation domain, and congruence mod $p$ of integer polynomials means equality there. Let $D$ be the determinant.

**Frobenius.** For $a,b,c\in\mathbb F_p$ and $L = ax+by+cz$: $L^p = a^px^p + b^py^p + c^pz^p = ax^p+by^p+cz^p$, because $(u+v)^p = u^p+v^p$ in characteristic $p$ (the middle binomial coefficients are divisible by $p$) and $a^p = a$ by Fermat. Applying this twice, $L^{p^2} = ax^{p^2}+by^{p^2}+cz^{p^2}$.

**Each nonzero linear form divides $D$.** Let $L\neq0$, say $c\ne0$ (the cases $b\ne0$ or $a\ne0$ are identical). Replacing the third column $C_3$ by $aC_1 + bC_2 + cC_3$ multiplies the determinant by $c$, and the new third column is $(L, L^p, L^{p^2})^T$ by the Frobenius identity. Expanding along it, $cD$ is a multiple of $L$; as $c$ is invertible, $L\mid D$.

**Enough distinct factors.** Consider the $1 + p + p^2$ forms
$$x;\qquad y+ix\ (i\in\mathbb F_p);\qquad z+ix+jy\ (i,j\in\mathbb F_p).$$
No two are proportional (scanning the variables in the order $z, y, x$, the first one with a nonzero coefficient has coefficient $1$; two distinct forms normalised this way cannot be scalar multiples of each other). Linear forms are irreducible, so these are pairwise non-associate primes of the UFD, all dividing $D$; hence their product
$$\Pi = x\prod_{i}(y+ix)\prod_{i,j}(z+ix+jy)$$
divides $D$, say $D = \Pi\cdot Q$.

**Comparing.** $D$ is homogeneous of degree $1+p+p^2$: it is the sum of the six monomials $\pm x^{e_1}y^{e_2}z^{e_3}$ with $(e_1,e_2,e_3)$ a permutation of $(1,p,p^2)$, which are distinct monomials, so $D\neq0$ and the coefficient of $xy^pz^{p^2}$ in $D$ is $1$ (from the diagonal). $\Pi$ also has degree $1+p+p^2$, so $Q$ is a nonzero constant. In $\Pi$, the monomial $xy^pz^{p^2}$ arises only by choosing $z$ in all $p^2$ factors $z+ix+jy$ (to reach $z^{p^2}$), then $y$ in all $p$ factors $y+ix$, then $x$: its coefficient is $1$. Hence $Q = 1$ and $D = \Pi$ in $\mathbb F_p[x,y,z]$.

Lifting $i,j$ to integers $0,\dots,p-1$, the determinant is congruent mod $p$ to
$$x\prod_{i=0}^{p-1}(y+ix)\prod_{i,j=0}^{p-1}(z+ix+jy),$$
a product of integer linear forms. ∎
